questions.question: In the southern hemisphere, a great circle track between two points at the same latitude will:-

options.text: curve towards the South Pole (appear to curve south of the rhumb line)
be identical to the rhumb line

questions.explanation: In the southern hemisphere, a great circle between two points at the same latitude curves towards the nearer pole (South Pole), passing south of the rhumb line (which follows the parallel of latitude). In the northern hemisphere, the great circle curves towards the North Pole. The great circle is always shorter than the rhumb line (except along the equator or meridians where they are equal).

questions.question: The primary purpose of dead reckoning (DR) navigation is:-

options.text: to determine the aircraft's position by calculating from a known position using heading, TAS, wind, and time
to use only radio navigation aids

questions.explanation: Dead reckoning (DR) is the process of calculating the aircraft's current position from a known starting position, using heading, TAS, wind velocity, and elapsed time. It is the fundamental navigation technique. DR is supplemented by map reading (visual fixes) and radio navigation to verify and update the calculated position.

questions.question: A fix in navigation is:-

options.text: a confirmed position obtained from two or more position lines or a visual identification of a known point

questions.explanation: A fix is a confirmed (reliable) position. It can be obtained from: (1) two or more intersecting position lines (VOR radials, NDB bearings, DME arcs), (2) a VOR/DME co-located station, (3) visual identification of a known ground feature, or (4) GPS. A fix is more reliable than a DR position, which is only calculated.

questions.question: An estimated position (EP) differs from a fix in that:-

options.text: it is based on incomplete information such as a single position line or uncertain DR calculation
it is always more accurate than a fix
it is the same as a fix

questions.explanation: An estimated position (EP) is less reliable than a fix. It may be based on: a single position line (the aircraft is somewhere along it), a DR calculation with uncertain wind, or a combination of incomplete information. On a chart, an EP is marked with a triangle, while a fix is marked with a circle.

questions.question: The track error angle after flying 30 nm and finding the aircraft 2 nm left of track is:-
questions.explanation: Using the 1-in-60 rule: Track Error = (distance off track / distance flown) × 60 = (2/30) × 60 = 4°. The aircraft has drifted 4° left of the planned track. To regain track, the pilot must alter heading to the right by the track error angle plus the closing angle.

questions.question: If the groundspeed check shows a groundspeed lower than planned, the pilot should:-

options.text: revise the ETA and check that fuel is sufficient for the revised flight time

questions.explanation: A lower-than-planned groundspeed means: (1) the flight will take longer than planned — revise the ETA and inform ATC, (2) more fuel will be consumed — check that remaining fuel is sufficient for the revised flight time plus reserves, (3) consider whether a diversion is necessary if fuel is marginal. Always monitor groundspeed and fuel state throughout the flight.

questions.question: The primary reference for measuring direction in aviation is:-

options.text: true north (geographic north) for chart work, magnetic north for flying

questions.explanation: In aviation, true north is the primary reference for chart work — tracks are measured as true bearings on the chart, then converted to magnetic for flying. Magnetic north is the reference used in the cockpit (compass, heading indicator, VOR radials, runway headings). The conversion between true and magnetic uses variation.

questions.question: The ISA pressure at sea level is:-
questions.explanation: The International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) defines sea level pressure as 1013.25 hPa (hectopascals) or 29.92 inches of mercury (inHg). This is the standard pressure setting used for flight levels. When the altimeter is set to 1013.25 hPa, it reads pressure altitude.

questions.question: The pressure change per 30 ft near sea level is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Near sea level, pressure decreases by approximately 1 hPa for every 30 ft of altitude gain (or 27 ft in some references). This relationship is used for quick pressure altitude calculations: Pressure Altitude = Elevation + (1013 - QNH) × 30. At higher altitudes, the rate decreases because air density decreases.

questions.question: Equivalent airspeed (EAS) is:-
questions.explanation: EAS is CAS corrected for compressibility of air. At low speeds and altitudes, the compressibility correction is negligible and EAS ≈ CAS. The full airspeed conversion chain is: IAS → (±instrument/position error) → CAS/RAS → (±compressibility) → EAS → (±density) → TAS. For PPL operations, compressibility is usually ignored.

questions.question: When homing to an NDB using the ADF, the pilot:-

options.text: keeps the ADF needle pointing to the nose (relative bearing 000°) by turning towards it
keeps the needle on the tail
keeps the needle on the left wing
ignores the needle and flies a compass heading

questions.explanation: Homing is the simplest form of NDB navigation — the pilot turns the aircraft until the ADF needle points to the nose (RB 000°) and keeps it there. The disadvantage is that in a crosswind, the aircraft will fly a curved path (longer than a straight track) because the pilot is constantly turning into the wind. Tracking is more efficient.

questions.question: When tracking TO an NDB in a crosswind, the ADF relative bearing should be:-

options.text: equal to the wind correction angle, on the upwind side

questions.explanation: When tracking (as opposed to homing), the pilot applies a wind correction angle (WCA). If the WCA is 10° right (heading 10° right of track), the ADF needle should show a relative bearing of 350° (10° left of the nose). The needle offset equals the WCA but on the opposite side. This maintains a straight track to the NDB.

questions.question: Station passage over a VOR is indicated by:-

options.text: the TO/FROM flag changing from TO to FROM and the CDI needle becoming erratic

questions.explanation: As the aircraft passes over (or very close to) a VOR, the TO/FROM flag changes from TO to FROM. The CDI needle may swing rapidly and become unreliable in the 'cone of confusion' directly above the station. Once past the station, the CDI settles and the FROM flag confirms the aircraft is now outbound.

questions.question: To intercept a VOR radial, the pilot should:-

options.text: set the desired radial on the OBI and fly a heading to intercept at an appropriate angle (typically 30° to 90°)
fly directly to the VOR first
set the OBI to the aircraft's heading

questions.explanation: To intercept a radial: (1) Set the desired radial on the OBI, (2) Determine which side of the radial you are on (CDI deflection), (3) Fly a heading that will intercept the radial at 30°-90° (smaller angles for close intercepts, larger for distant), (4) As the CDI centres, turn to track the radial.

questions.question: The cone of confusion above a VOR station is the area where:-

options.text: the VOR signal is unreliable and the CDI and TO/FROM flag may give erratic indications

questions.explanation: The cone of confusion (or cone of ambiguity) is the airspace directly above a VOR where the signal is unreliable. The CDI needle swings erratically and the TO/FROM flag may oscillate. The size of the cone increases with altitude. Pilots should not attempt to navigate using VOR indications while in the cone of confusion.

questions.question: The squawk code 7700 on a transponder indicates:-
questions.explanation: Transponder emergency codes: 7700 = Emergency/Distress, 7600 = Radio (communication) failure, 7500 = Hijack/unlawful interference. Squawking 7700 alerts ATC that the aircraft is in an emergency situation and triggers special attention on the radar display.

questions.question: The squawk code 7600 on a transponder indicates:-
questions.explanation: Squawk 7600 indicates radio (communication) failure. If a pilot loses radio communication, they should squawk 7600 to alert ATC. The pilot should then follow the published radio failure procedures: continue on the last assigned route and altitude, or if VFR, land at the nearest suitable aerodrome.

questions.question: The squawk code 7500 on a transponder indicates:-
questions.explanation: Squawk 7500 indicates hijack or unlawful interference with the aircraft. This code should only be set if the aircraft is being subjected to unlawful interference. ATC will take special action upon detecting this code. Never set 7500 accidentally — if set in error, immediately change it and inform ATC.

questions.question: The heading conversion sequence from True to Compass is:-
questions.explanation: The conversion sequence: True ± Variation = Magnetic ± Deviation = Compass. Memory aid: 'True Virgins Make Dull Companions' (TVMDC). Going T→C: add West, subtract East for both variation and deviation. Going C→T: reverse the signs. This is the fundamental heading conversion used in all navigation.

questions.question: An aircraft at position S26°00' E028°00' needs to fly to S28°00' E028°00'. The distance is approximately:-
questions.explanation: Both positions are on the same meridian (E028°00'), so the distance is purely a change in latitude. Change in latitude = 28° - 26° = 2°. Distance = 2° × 60 nm/° = 120 nm. When two positions share the same longitude, the distance calculation is straightforward using the latitude difference.

questions.question: The variation in the Johannesburg area of South Africa is approximately:-
questions.explanation: In the Johannesburg area, magnetic variation is approximately 20° West (this changes slowly over time due to secular change). Across South Africa, variation ranges from about 17°W in the east to about 27°W in the west. Always check the current isogonal on the chart for the specific area of flight.

questions.question: When using a GPS for VFR navigation, the pilot must:-

options.text: still carry current charts and be able to navigate by conventional means if the GPS fails
not use any other navigation method

questions.explanation: GPS is an excellent navigation aid but must not be the sole means of navigation for VFR flights. The pilot must carry current charts, be proficient in map reading and DR navigation, and be able to navigate safely if the GPS fails. GPS should supplement, not replace, conventional navigation skills.

questions.question: The term 'RAIM' in GPS navigation stands for:-
questions.explanation: RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) is a GPS function that checks the integrity of the satellite signals. It compares position solutions from different satellite combinations to detect any faulty satellite. RAIM requires at least 5 satellites (6 for fault exclusion). If RAIM is not available, the GPS position may be unreliable.

questions.question: The QDM of an NDB is:-

options.text: the magnetic bearing TO the NDB from the aircraft
the magnetic bearing FROM the NDB
the true bearing to the NDB
the relative bearing of the NDB

questions.explanation: QDM = magnetic bearing TO the station (the heading to fly to reach the NDB in zero wind). QDR = magnetic bearing FROM the station (reciprocal of QDM). QTE = true bearing FROM the station. QUJ = true bearing TO the station. QDM = Magnetic Heading + Relative Bearing (subtract 360° if >360°).

questions.question: The QDR of an NDB is:-

options.text: the magnetic bearing FROM the NDB to the aircraft
the magnetic bearing TO the NDB
the true bearing from the NDB

questions.explanation: QDR = magnetic bearing FROM the NDB (the reciprocal of QDM). QDR = QDM ± 180°. The QDR is the bearing to plot FROM the NDB on the chart to show the aircraft's position line. For example, if QDM = 270°, then QDR = 270° - 180° = 090°.

questions.question: When flying in the circuit at an uncontrolled aerodrome, the circuit altitude is typically:-
questions.explanation: The standard circuit height is 1000 ft above aerodrome elevation (AAL). Some aerodromes may specify different circuit heights — check the AIP or aerodrome information. Circuit altitude (AMSL) = aerodrome elevation + 1000 ft. Use QNH to maintain circuit altitude or QFE to maintain circuit height.

questions.question: The minimum altitude for VFR flight over a congested area (city, town) is:-

options.text: 1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 600 m of the aircraft

questions.explanation: Over congested areas (cities, towns, settlements), the minimum height is 1000 ft above the highest obstacle within a radius of 600 m from the aircraft. Over non-congested areas, the minimum is 500 ft above the ground or water, or 500 ft above the highest obstacle within 600 m. These are minimum heights — higher is safer.

questions.question: The minimum altitude for VFR flight over non-congested areas is:-

options.text: 500 ft above the ground or water, or 500 ft above the highest obstacle within 600 m

questions.explanation: Over non-congested areas, the minimum height for VFR flight is 500 ft above the ground or water, or 500 ft above the highest obstacle within a radius of 600 m of the aircraft. This ensures a reasonable margin for emergency landing and avoids disturbance to people and property on the ground.

questions.question: A pilot flying at FL055 with an OAT of +10°C. The TAS if the CAS is 100 kts is approximately:-
questions.explanation: At FL055 (5500 ft), using the approximate rule of 2% per 1000 ft: TAS ≈ CAS × (1 + 0.02 × 5.5) = 100 × 1.11 = 111 kts ≈ 110 kts. The warmer-than-ISA temperature slightly increases TAS further. Using the navigation computer with pressure altitude 5500 ft and OAT +10°C gives a more precise answer.

questions.question: The purpose of the AIRAC (Aeronautical Information Regulation and Control) cycle is:-

options.text: to ensure aeronautical information changes are published on fixed dates (every 28 days) for advance planning

questions.explanation: AIRAC is an internationally agreed system where significant aeronautical information changes are published on fixed 28-day cycle dates. This allows pilots and operators to receive, process, and implement changes in advance. AIRAC effective dates are published years in advance. Changes include: new procedures, airspace amendments, and navaid changes.

questions.question: The wind side of the navigation computer is used to find:-

options.text: heading, groundspeed, drift, and wind velocity from the triangle of velocities

questions.explanation: The wind side of the navigation computer solves the triangle of velocities. Given track, TAS, and wind, it finds heading and groundspeed. Given heading, TAS, and track/groundspeed, it finds wind velocity. It can also find drift angle. The wind side uses a rotating compass rose and a sliding grid.

questions.question: The calculator side of the navigation computer is used for:-

options.text: time/speed/distance, fuel calculations, unit conversions, and TAS from CAS

questions.explanation: The calculator side is a circular slide rule used for: time/speed/distance problems, fuel consumption calculations, unit conversions (nm/km/sm, litres/gallons, kg/lbs), TAS from CAS (using the airspeed window with altitude and temperature), density altitude, and any multiplication/division problems.

questions.question: The recommended pre-flight navigation planning sequence is:-

options.text: weather check, NOTAMs, chart preparation, track measurement, heading/groundspeed calculation, fuel planning, flight plan filing
file flight plan first, then check weather

questions.explanation: Pre-flight planning sequence: (1) Check weather (TAFs, METARs, area forecasts, winds aloft), (2) Check NOTAMs, (3) Prepare charts (draw tracks, mark waypoints), (4) Measure tracks and distances, (5) Calculate headings and groundspeeds using forecast winds, (6) Calculate fuel required (including reserves), (7) Complete the flight log, (8) File a flight plan if required.
